cim: 10 artificial intelligence graduate programs from U.S. News' list of 22
cim_eredeti: 10 artificial intelligence graduate programs from U.S. News' list of 22
szoveg_eredeti:
See tuition, enrollment, and deadlines for 10 artificial intelligence graduate programs from U.S. News' 2026 ranking of 22.

Anyone weighing a graduate degree in artificial intelligence faces a choice with years of study and a hefty bill attached. The discipline sits where several fields meet, and the program a student picks shapes which of those fields that student will master. A school with deep engineering roots may steer coursework in one direction, and a department grounded in computer science may pull it in another. Applicants juggle practical constraints such as location, cohort size, and the calendar of application deadlines. A poor match drains money and months that a first job or a career switch could have claimed. Reputation offers a starting point, yet it says little about what a particular program costs or how crowded its classrooms run.

Price draws the sharpest dividing line. Annual master's tuition at leading schools can differ by tens of thousands of dollars, a spread that can decide whether a degree fits a family's budget. Most institutions publish a yearly rate, some add a per-credit charge for part-time students, and one posts only the per-credit figure, which complicates any side-by-side comparison. Size introduces a second variable. One department may enroll a few hundred full-time students, and another may hold many times that number. Students who judge schools by name recognition alone miss these trade-offs and the spending tied to them.

U.S. News published its 2026 ranking of artificial intelligence graduate programs as a specialty within its Best Computer Science Schools list. The publication describes these programs as requiring broad training that draws on computer science, cognitive psychology, and engineering. Its specialty list spans 22 programs, and this article covers the 10 in first through 10th place. Each entry reports master's tuition and fees, full-time enrollment, location, and the school's position in the broader computer science ranking, and several add a department name, an application deadline, or an application fee. The publication outlines its approach on a separate methodology page, which falls outside this article, and it keeps average quantitative GRE scores behind its Grad Compass tool.

Carnegie Mellon University holds the first spot among artificial intelligence graduate programs and shares the top position in the wider computer science list, a three-way tie with two other schools. The Pittsburgh university's command of the specialty mirrors its standing across the discipline as a whole. Its School of Computer Science handles applications and closes the window on Dec. 10. The cutoff arrives five days ahead of the Dec. 15 date that four of the five other programs with a stated deadline use. Stanford's Dec. 2 date is the lone earlier one. Applicants spreading files across several schools should schedule the Carnegie Mellon packet among their first.

A full-time master's student pays $61,406 a year in tuition and fees. Carnegie Mellon prices a part-time route at $1,845 per credit, an option for students who cannot commit to a full-time schedule. At the per-credit rate, a part-timer would need about 33 credits before the bill matched one full-time year. Three of the 10 programs post both a full-time and a per-credit price, and Carnegie Mellon belongs to that group. The pairing lets prospective students weigh the two paths side by side.

Carnegie Mellon enrolls 1,887 full-time students, 1,056 more than MIT. Illinois stands as the one school among the 10 with a larger full-time body. A cohort of that size gives each student a deep pool of classmates to learn alongside.

Carnegie Mellon teams with its Pittsburgh neighbor on a brain-science hub. The university operates the Center for the Neural Basis of Cognition in partnership with the University of Pittsburgh, and the center hosts computational neuroscience training in a cross-disciplinary setting. Graduate options there include a Ph.D. in Neural Computation, along with combined doctorates linking to Carnegie Mellon's Department of Statistics and its Machine Learning Department. The doctoral tracks extend Carnegie Mellon's computing strength into the study of the brain and cognition, reaching past the boundaries of one school.

Massachusetts Institute of Technology claims second place in artificial intelligence while charging $62,396 a year in full-time master's tuition and fees and enrolling 831 full-time students. MIT shares first place in Best Computer Science Schools with Carnegie Mellon University and Stanford University, and its student body is the smallest of those three co-leaders. Its annual bill runs $990 above Carnegie Mellon's. Stanford asks $3,469 more than MIT for a full-time year.

Cost does little to separate MIT from Carnegie Mellon. Class size draws the sharper contrast, and MIT's cohort trails by a wide margin. MIT posts no part-time per-credit rate. Its full-time price is the only cost figure on the listing, which leaves part-time students without a published benchmark.

The Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science houses the degree, placing both disciplines in a single academic unit. The department defines artificial intelligence and decision-making as a field that borrows from each of them. Work in the area aims to build systems that perceive, communicate, and act in the outside world as they learn and adapt.

MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory pursues research in computing and AI, with artificial intelligence and systems among its focus areas. The lab stands as the largest at MIT that draws on several departments, according to the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing. Its agenda centers on foundational inquiry and on inventing new core technologies for computing.

Health care forms another strand of AI work tied to the department. The Jameel Clinic concentrates on AI and health. Groups at IMES, CSAIL, LIDS, and the Eric and Wendy Schmidt Center at the Broad Institute apply AI to health care and the life sciences as well.

Four of the eight programs below MIT in the specialty list count more full-time students: Stanford, Georgia Tech, Illinois, and UC San Diego. Headcount, on this evidence, does not decide where a program lands.

Stanford University's Department of Computer Science stops accepting applications on Dec. 2, the earliest cutoff among the deadlines these 10 listings state. Carnegie Mellon University gives applicants eight more days. Four other programs in the group, at Georgia Tech, Texas--Austin, Cornell, and Washington, hold their windows open until Dec. 15. Anyone whose shortlist includes Stanford must finish that file 13 days ahead of the mid-December cluster and build the rest of the application calendar around the Stanford date.

Full-time master's students at Stanford pay $65,865 a year in tuition and fees, the second-steepest annual bill among the nine programs that publish a full-time figure. The total runs $3,469 above MIT's and $4,459 above Carnegie Mellon's. Only Cornell charges more, and its rate exceeds Stanford's by $9,519. Stanford, MIT, and Carnegie Mellon share first place in the broader computer science standings, and Stanford sets the price ceiling for that group.

Stanford outprices the two other California schools in this group by a wide margin. Berkeley's bill comes in $27,973 lower per year, and UC San Diego's comes in $35,566 lower. A student set on staying in California faces a five-figure yearly gap without crossing a state line, and each added year of study at Stanford widens the cumulative difference.

Stanford counts 1,004 full-time students, 173 more than MIT and 883 fewer than Carnegie Mellon. Among the three computer science co-leaders, Stanford sits in the middle on size while carrying the highest price.
